name: primesieve
why: Fast prime generator that lets you count primes to enormous limits and explore number theory at home.

brief.what_it_is: primesieve is a command-line program and C/C++ library for quickly generating prime numbers. You give it a range, such as primesieve 1e10 to count primes up to 10 billion, and it prints the count. With --print it lists the primes, and with --count=2 or --print=2 it counts or prints twin primes (k-tuplets up to 6 are supported). It can handle limits up to 2^64, and it also has a built-in CPU and RAM stress test.
brief.why_it_exists: The README frames it as a fast, cache-efficient way to generate primes and prime k-tuplets to very large limits, using all CPU cores when ordering does not matter. The scout notes describe it as a way to count primes to enormous limits and explore number theory at home.
brief.how_it_works: It uses the segmented sieve of Eratosthenes with wheel factorization, with run time O(n log log n) and memory O(sqrt n). For primes above 2^32 it uses the bucket sieve to improve cache efficiency. It detects the CPU's L1 and L2 cache sizes and sizes its data structures to match, using about 8 bytes per sieving prime per thread.

commands_seen.context: Counts the primes up to 1e10 using all CPU cores (the default action is counting).

Stores the primes up to 1000000 in a text file via shell redirection.
Prints the twin primes up to 1000000.
Counts the prime triplets inside the interval [1e10, 1e10+2^32].
Runs the CPU stress test for five minutes; it checks prime counts on large ranges and reports OK per block, ending with All tests passed successfully!

brief.install_notes: The README lists package-manager installs: winget install primesieve (Windows), brew install primesieve (macOS), sudo pacman -S primesieve (Arch), sudo apt install primesieve (Debian/Ubuntu), sudo dnf install primesieve (Fedora), pkg install primesieve (FreeBSD), and sudo zypper install primesieve (openSUSE). For development with libprimesieve, install libprimesieve-dev or libprimesieve-devel. Building from source needs a C++ compiler supporting C++14 or later and CMake 3.9 or newer, then cmake ., cmake --build . --parallel, sudo cmake --install ., and sudo ldconfig. Detailed steps are in doc/BUILD.md. No accounts or special hardware are mentioned. The RAM stress test needs about 1.2 GiB per thread.
brief.standout: The program sizes its sieve from the CPU's measured cache sizes, and it ships a stress test that uses prime counting over huge ranges as a workload. Each block has a known answer, so a miscalculation points to a hardware fault, which makes it a practical way to check cooling and stability.
brief.status: Looks maintained, but the fetched README has no release date or commit date. The README has active CI and benchmark badges, a stress-test sample output dated Apr 12, and a sponsor section that says the author is still maintaining it. Packaged across many distributions. Status is unknown beyond that evidence.
brief.caveats: Printing and writing to a file run single-threaded because output must be in order, and they use the standard output path rather than file-specific I/O. The README says that for maximum throughput you should use libprimesieve in memory instead. Source builds need a C++14 compiler and CMake 3.9 or newer. The RAM stress mode uses about 1.2 GiB per thread. The stress test's default timeout is 24 hours. The README does not state a license, and I did not check the LICENSE file.
quotes: primesieve is a command-line program and C/C++ library for quickly generating prime numbers.
It is very cache efficient, it detects your CPU's L1 & L2 cache sizes and allocates its main data structures accordingly.
primesieve's stress test supports two modes: **CPU** (highest CPU load, uses little memory) and **RAM** (high memory usage, uses about 1.2 GiB per thread).
